questions.modelAnswer: Toward the positive anode.
requiredPoints: Toward the positive anode.

questions.text: What group is present on the alpha carbon of amino acids in any protein?
questions.explanation: The alpha carbon of a standard amino acid carries amino and carboxyl groups, a side chain and hydrogen; Glycine has two hydrogens, and proline has a cyclic secondary amino group.

questions.text: Amino acids are ampholytes because they can function as either a(n):
questions.explanation: Amino acids contain proton-accepting amino groups and proton-donating carboxyl groups, enabling acid and base behavior.

questions.text: The zwitter ion is:
questions.explanation: A zwitterion carries both positive and negative formal charges in the same molecule. At the isoelectric point these balance to give zero net charge, without eliminating the individual charges.

questions.text: The 21st amino acid is:
questions.explanation: Selenocysteine can be genetically incorporated using a stop-codon-recognizing tRNA and is called the 21st proteinogenic amino acid.

questions.text: Proteins are amphoteric.
questions.explanation: Carboxyl groups donate protons and amino or basic side-chain groups accept them, so the protein can behave as an acid or a base.
questions.modelAnswer: Proteins contain acidic and basic ionizable groups; They can donate or accept protons depending on pH.
requiredPoints: Proteins contain acidic and basic ionizable groups
They can donate or accept protons depending on pH.

questions.explanation: Condensation forms bonds between building blocks with loss of water; hydrolysis is the reverse process that breaks them apart.

are synthesized from monomers by dehydration reactions.
are synthesized as a result of peptide bond formation between monomers.
are decomposed into their subunits by dehydration reactions.

questions.text: Which pair of amino acids absorbs the most UV light at 280 nm?
questions.explanation: Tryptophan and tyrosine absorb strongly near 280 nm; the other listed pairs lack comparable aromatic chromophores.

questions.text: Which of the following is the unique part of each amino acid?
questions.explanation: The R group differs between amino acids and determines their characteristic properties; amino and carboxyl groups are shared backbone features.

questions.text: Amino acids used to build proteins in cells can be distinguished through
questions.explanation: The R groups distinguish amino acids because the alpha-amino and alpha-carboxyl backbone groups are otherwise shared.

questions.text: There are four parts to each amino acid. A carbon atom is bonded to a hydrogen atom, R group, and functional groups are : 6
questions.explanation: The alpha carbon of a typical amino acid bears an amino group, a carboxyl group, hydrogen and an R group.

questions.text: There are _ common amino acids derived from human proteins?
questions.explanation: The standard universal genetic code specifies twenty common amino acids; rare selenocysteine incorporation is a separate recoding mechanism.

questions.text: There are four parts to each amino acid. A carbon atom is bonded to a hydrogen atom, R group, and functional groups are :
questions.explanation: A typical alpha carbon is attached to amino and carboxyl functional groups plus hydrogen and the variable R group.

questions.text: There are common amino acids derived from human proteins?
questions.explanation: Twenty common amino acids are encoded by the universal genetic code; unusual selenocysteine uses a special recoding mechanism.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about proteins?
questions.explanation: A protein is a polymer of amino-acid residues linked by peptide bonds; glucose instead forms carbohydrate polymers.
options: Proteins are polymers of amino acids
Proteins are polymers of peptide bonds
Proteins are polymers of disulfide bridges

questions.text: Which part of the amino acid gives it uniqueness?
questions.explanation: The side chain varies among amino acids and determines their chemical differences; the amino and carboxyl groups are common features.

questions.text: The simplest amino acid with hydrogen atom as an R-group is
questions.explanation: Glycine's side chain is a single hydrogen, making it the simplest amino acid and the only achiral standard residue.

questions.text: alpha-carbon of amino acids is chiral, except
questions.explanation: Glycine has two hydrogens attached to its alpha carbon, so that carbon has no four distinct substituents and is achiral.

questions.text: All amino acids have enantiomer except
questions.explanation: Glycine is achiral because its alpha carbon bears two identical hydrogen substituents; the other amino acids have enantiomers.

questions.text: Proteins absorb lights at wave length 280nm, due to presence of which amino acid
questions.explanation: Tryptophan has an aromatic indole chromophore that absorbs near 280 nm; lysine and glycine do not account for this protein absorption.

questions.text: Diet proteins are important as they are the main source for
questions.explanation: Protein is the principal dietary source of amino nitrogen and supplies sulfur in methionine/cysteine. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are also abundant in carbohydrate and fat, so their combinations are less specific. Nonprotein sulfate can contribute sulfur as well.

questions.text: at pii above isoelectric point, amino acids show
questions.explanation: Above its isoelectric point an amino acid has net negative charge and moves toward the positive anode.

questions.text: at pH below isoelectric point, amino acids show
questions.explanation: Below its isoelectric point an amino acid is more protonated, carries net positive charge and moves toward the negative cathode.

questions.text: Amino acids are ampholytes because they can function as either an):
questions.explanation: Amino and carboxyl groups permit amino acids to accept or donate protons, so they function as bases or acids.

questions.text: The 21st amino acid is:
questions.explanation: Selenocysteine is called the twenty-first proteinogenic amino acid because a specialized tRNA permits its incorporation at recoded UGA; hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine arise by modification of existing residues.

questions.text: The 21st amino acid is:
questions.explanation: Selenocysteine uses a specialized tRNA and recoding mechanism for incorporation into proteins; hydroxylysine and hydroxyproline are formed by modifying lysine and proline after translation.

questions.text: On biochemical basis explain: At the isoelectric point (IEP), the amino acid cannot migrate in electric field.
questions.explanation: Positive and negative molecular charges balance at the isoelectric pH, removing the net electrical driving force.
questions.modelAnswer: At the isoelectric pH the amino acid has zero net charge; It therefore has no net electrophoretic migration toward either electrode
requiredPoints: At the isoelectric pH the amino acid has zero net charge
It therefore has no net electrophoretic migration toward either electrode

questions.text: Proteins act as a blood buffer mains due to the residue of which amino acid:-
questions.explanation: Histidine imidazole groups can accept and donate protons around physiological pH and therefore contribute to protein buffering.

questions.text: Which of the following is a Nitrogen containing compounds
questions.explanation: Alanine contains an amino nitrogen; glucose, glycerol, palmitate and phosphatidic acid do not contain nitrogen in their basic structures.

questions.text: at pH above isoelectric point, amino acids show
questions.explanation: At a pH above pI the molecule is more deprotonated, giving a net negative charge and anodal migration.

questions.text: At a pH greater than its isoelectric point (pI), a protein has:
questions.explanation: At pH above its isoelectric point a protein becomes net negatively charged because deprotonation predominates.

questions.text: Which property is common to the standard amino acids incorporated into proteins?
questions.explanation: Protein amino acids are alpha amino acids; glycine is achiral, so all-L or all-optically-active claims are not strictly true.

questions.text: Which of the following is a nitrogen-containing compound ?
questions.explanation: Alanine contains an alpha-amino nitrogen; the other listed basic molecular structures contain carbon, oxygen and hydrogen without nitrogen.

questions.text: At a pH greater than the pI of a protein, it will have:
questions.explanation: Above its isoelectric pH, a protein has a net negative charge and tends to migrate toward the positive anode.
options: Protein will precipitate from the solution
Protein will migrate towards the cathodes

questions.text: Diet proteins are the main source of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Dietary proteins provide amino nitrogen and sulfur-containing amino acids. The other element pairs are also supplied abundantly by nonprotein macronutrients.

questions.text: Diet proteins are the main source of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Proteins supply amino nitrogen and sulfur through methionine/cysteine. Carbohydrates and lipids also supply carbon, hydrogen and oxygen; nonprotein sulfate can also contribute sulfur.

questions.text: Protein act as a buffer mainly due to which amino acid residue?
questions.explanation: Histidine's imidazole titrates near physiological pH, allowing proton acceptance and donation that contributes to protein buffering.

questions.text: DNA codes for 20 different amino acids. Which of the following is responsible } for making each of the amino acids different from one another?
questions.explanation: Different amino-acid side chains or R groups determine their distinct chemical properties; the common amino and carboxyl groups do not distinguish them.

questions.text: Atneutral PH a mixture of amino acids in solution would be predominantly:
questions.explanation: Free amino acids commonly carry a protonated alpha-amino group and deprotonated alpha-carboxyl group at neutral pH, giving a dipolar zwitterionic form.

questions.text: Most of the ultraviolet absorption of proteins at 280 nm is due to their content of:
questions.explanation: Tryptophan contributes strongly to protein absorbance near 280 nm through its indole chromophore; none of the other four amino acids has an aromatic chromophore.

questions.text: Mammalian Proteins contain
questions.explanation: Chiral standard residues in mammalian ribosomally synthesized proteins have L configuration. Glycine is achiral and has no D/L designation.

questions.text: An amino acid not found in proteins is
questions.explanation: Beta-alanine has its amino group on the beta carbon and is outside the standard ribosomal alpha-amino-acid set; proline, lysine and histidine are standard protein residues.

questions.text: The greatest buffering capacity at physiological pH of plasma would be provided by a protein rich in which of the following amino acids?
questions.explanation: Histidine's imidazole pKa lies relatively near physiological pH and enables substantial proton buffering compared with the other side chains.

questions.text: If the amino group and a carboxylic group of the amino acid are attached to same carbon atom, the amino acid is called
questions.explanation: In an alpha-amino acid, the amino group attaches to the alpha-carbon immediately adjacent to the carboxyl group.

questions.text: The true statement about solutions of amino acids at physiological pH is
questions.explanation: At physiological pH the alpha-amino group is generally protonated and alpha-carboxyl group deprotonated, so amino acids carry both charge types even if side chains alter net charge.
options: All amino acids contain both positive and negative charges
All amino acids contain positively charged side chains
Some amino acids contain only positive charge
All amino acids contain negatively charged side chains

questions.text: At a low hydrogen-ion concentration (pH above their pI), amino acids carry which net charge and migrate toward which electrode?
questions.explanation: Low hydrogen-ion concentration means high pH; above pI amino acids are net negative and migrate toward the anode.

questions.text: Atalow PH, amino acids will carry......charge, and migrate to...
questions.explanation: Low pH favors protonation and net positive charge, causing migration toward the negative cathode.

questions.text: In electrophoresis, an amino acid moves towards the anode:
questions.explanation: Above its pI, the amino acid has a net negative charge and migrates toward the positive anode.
options: At pH equal to its isoelectric point
At pH higher than its isoelectric point
At pH lower than its isoelectric point

questions.text: All the followings are true about Zwitter lon EXCEPT
questions.explanation: At pI the amino acid has zero net charge and shows no net electrophoretic migration, despite carrying both positive and negative groups.
options: Is formed at the isoelectric point
Is formed at a specific pH for each amino acid
Migrates to the cathode in an electric field

questions.text: The repeating units of protein?
questions.explanation: Proteins are polymers of amino-acid residues; nucleotides form nucleic acids and glucose units form polysaccharides.

questions.text: An amino acid which does not have a specific genetic code is
questions.explanation: Hydroxyproline is formed by post-translational hydroxylation of proline and has no separate standard genetic-code codon.

questions.text: Aliphatic amino acids:

questions.text: Which two amino acids have a net positive charge at pH 7?

Arginine

questions.text: What character is used to classify amino acids?
questions.explanation: Side-chain chemistry determines solubility, interactions and common amino-acid categories.

requiredPoints: The chemical properties of their side chains (R groups), especially polarity and charge.

questions.text: Which amino acids are aromatic?
questions.explanation: Aromatic rings distinguish these residues; polarity differs because tyrosine contains a hydroxyl group.

requiredPoints: Phenylalanine
Tyrosine
Tryptophan

questions.text: Which essential amino acid is nonpolar?

questions.text: Which of the following is a sulfhydryl-containing amino acid?
questions.explanation: Cysteine has a free sulfhydryl side chain; cystine contains a disulfide and methionine contains a thioether.

questions.text: Which of the following is a branched amino acid?
questions.explanation: Isoleucine has a branched hydrocarbon side chain; cysteine, proline and histidine do not belong to the branched-chain group.

questions.text: Serine and threonine are polar amino acids due to:
questions.explanation: Serine and threonine contain side-chain hydroxyl groups that hydrogen-bond with water.
options: Reactive hydroxyl group in the side chain.
Reactive thiol group in the side chain.
Reactive amide group in the side chain.
Reactive carboxyl group in the side chain.

questions.text: The two amino acids that contain sulfur atoms are:
questions.explanation: Cysteine contains a thiol and methionine a thioether; serine and threonine contain hydroxyl groups rather than sulfur.

questions.text: Which of the following is an a-imino acid?
questions.explanation: Proline has a secondary alpha amine within a ring and is traditionally classified as an imino acid.

questions.text: Which of the following amino acids contain a heterocyclic ring?
questions.explanation: Histidine contains an imidazole ring with nitrogen heteroatoms; the other choices have no ring.

questions.text: All of the following are hydroxy-containing amino acids except:
questions.explanation: Valine has a branched hydrocarbon side chain; serine, threonine and tyrosine possess hydroxyl groups.

questions.text: Lysine is a:
questions.explanation: Lysine has a basic side chain and is exclusively ketogenic, yielding ketone-body precursors rather than net glucose precursors.

questions.text: The two amino acids that are purely ketogenic are:
questions.explanation: Lysine and leucine are exclusively ketogenic; isoleucine has both glucogenic and ketogenic products and valine is glucogenic.

questions.text: Sulphur containing amino acids are:
questions.explanation: Cysteine and methionine contain sulfur; hydroxyl-bearing threonine and serine do not.

questions.text: Amino acids with hydroxyl groups are:
questions.explanation: Serine and threonine have hydroxyl-bearing side chains; alanine, valine and isoleucine have hydrocarbon side chains.

questions.text: All of the following are polar amino acids Except:
questions.explanation: Alanine has a methyl side chain; glutamate and arginine are charged and serine is polar through its hydroxyl group.

questions.text: Acidic amino acids include:
questions.explanation: Aspartate and glutamate each contain a side-chain carboxylate, making them acidic amino acids.

questions.text: The following are basic amino acids:
questions.explanation: Histidine, lysine and arginine have basic nitrogen-containing side chains; the other combinations include neutral residues.

questions.text: Branched chain amino acids include:
questions.explanation: Leucine, isoleucine and valine are the branched-chain amino acids; threonine and methionine are separate groups.

questions.text: A nonessential amino acid containing sulfur is:
questions.explanation: Cysteine is ordinarily synthesized in humans and contains sulfur; methionine is sulfur-containing but essential.

questions.text: Two essential amino acids: one containing sulfur and one branched.

questions.text: Two sulfur containing amino acids: one essential and one non-essential.

questions.modelAnswer: Methionine is essential; Cysteine is ordinarily nonessential.
requiredPoints: Methionine is essential
Cysteine is ordinarily nonessential.

questions.text: Two hydroxyl- containing amino acids.
questions.explanation: Both have hydroxyl-bearing side chains that hydrogen-bond with water; tyrosine is another acceptable hydroxyl-containing example.

Threonine.

questions.text: Two sulfur containing amino acids.

Methionine.

questions.text: Two aromatic amino acids.

Tryptophan.

questions.text: Four essential amino acids.

Leucine

questions.text: A semi-essential amino acid.

questions.text: Two pure glucogenic amino acids.
questions.explanation: Alanine yields pyruvate and aspartate yields oxaloacetate, which can form glucose without a ketogenic carbon product.

Aspartate.

questions.text: Two pure ketogenic amino acids.

Lysine.

questions.text: Two non polar amino acids.

Valine.

questions.text: Two polar amino acids with uncharged groups. IV- On Biochemical basis explain:

Threonine.

questions.text: Some amino acids are polar although having uncharged (R) groups.

questions.text: Arginine is a semi-essential amino acid.

questions.text: Essential & non essential amino acids (definition, example).

questions.text: Proline amino acid:

questions.text: Amino acid which we obtains from food and our bodies are unable to build it is:
questions.explanation: Phenylalanine requires dietary supply in humans; alanine, glycine and serine are ordinarily synthesized.

questions.text: CAMP Activates which of the following enzymes?

questions.text: All the following used in glucagon Signal Termination except
questions.explanation: Phosphodiesterase hydrolyzes cAMP and reduces activation of protein kinase A. Inhibiting phosphodiesterase therefore prolongs rather than terminates glucagon signaling.

questions.explanation: Adenylyl cyclase cyclizes ATP to cAMP with release of pyrophosphate. Phosphodiesterase performs the opposite signaling role by hydrolyzing cAMP to AMP.

questions.explanation: G6P inhibits hexokinase, not glucokinase. Hepatic glucokinase is insulin inducible and has high capacity; hexokinase has higher glucose affinity.
options: Glucokinase is induced by insulin during the well-fed state

questions.text: All the following statements are true except
questions.explanation: In the hepatic context implied by insulin induction, pyruvate kinase is inhibited by phosphorylation and ATP, and activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.
options: Pyruvate kinase is active in phosphorylated form
Pyruvate kinase is inhibited by high ATP
Pyruvate kinase is activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
Pyruvate kinase is induced by insulin

questions.text: Which of the following reactions produces ATP by substrate level phosphorylation?
questions.explanation: Pyruvate kinase transfers the PEP phosphate directly to ADP. The other listed steps do not form ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation.
options: Conversion of glucose into glucose 6 phosphate
Conversion of fructose 6 phosphate to fructose 1,6 bis phosphate
Conversion of glyceraldehyde 3 phosphate into 1,3 bisphosphoglycerate

questions.text: Which of the following is the end product of glycolysis in a vigorously contracting skeletal muscle?
questions.explanation: Vigorous contracting muscle increases conversion of pyruvate to lactate, regenerating NAD+ for glycolysis.

questions.text: Which of the following enzymes of the glycolytic pathway can be inhibited by fluoride?
questions.explanation: Enolase removes water from 2-phosphoglycerate to form phosphoenolpyruvate in glycolysis. Fluoride inhibits this step, which explains its traditional use to reduce glycolysis in blood specimens.

questions.text: Which of the following enzymes are regulatory enzymes of glycolysis in skeletal muscles?
questions.explanation: PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase both regulate muscle glycolysis. The alternative pairs contain nonregulatory enzymes or hepatic glucokinase.

questions.text: Which of the following enzymes of the glycolytic pathway is induced by insulin?
questions.explanation: Insulin induces hepatic glucokinase in the fed state. Pyruvate dehydrogenase is outside glycolysis and the other choices are not the standard inducible glucose-trapping enzyme.

questions.text: Which of the following is the end product of glycolysis in skeletal muscle during severe muscular exercise?
questions.explanation: During severe exercise, reduction of pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD+ so anaerobic glycolysis can continue.

questions.text: How many net ATP molecules are produced during anaerobic glycolysis?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis forms four ATP but uses two ATP in its investment phase, leaving two net ATP per glucose. Conversion of pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD+ without producing additional ATP.

questions.text: Which of the following glycolytic enzymes is responsible for production of NAD+?
questions.explanation: Lactate dehydrogenase reoxidizes NADH to NAD+ when it converts pyruvate to lactate, supporting continued anaerobic glycolysis.

questions.text: Which of the following is a glycolytic enzyme?
questions.explanation: Enolase converts 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate in cytosolic glycolysis. Aconitase and citrate synthase belong to the TCA cycle, while pyruvate carboxylase supports gluconeogenesis and replenishment of oxaloacetate.

questions.text: Two compounds containing high energy phosphate bonds
questions.explanation: Phosphoenolpyruvate transfers phosphate to ADP during glycolysis; 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate does the same through phosphoglycerate kinase.
questions.modelAnswer: Phosphoenolpyruvate transfers phosphate to ADP during glycolysis; 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate does the same through phosphoglycerate kinase.
requiredPoints: Phosphoenolpyruvate transfers phosphate to ADP during glycolysis
1,3-bisphosphoglycerate does the same through phosphoglycerate kinase.

questions.text: The enzymes of glycolysis are located in the:
questions.explanation: Glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate using cytosolic enzymes. It can therefore generate ATP in mature erythrocytes, which have no mitochondria.

questions.text: For every one molecule of sugar glucose which is oxidized molecule of pyruvic acid are produced.
questions.explanation: The six-carbon glucose skeleton is split into two three-carbon trioses, each of which becomes pyruvate. Glycolysis itself releases no carbon dioxide.

questions.text: The rate limiting enzyme for glycolysis is:
questions.explanation: PFK-1 converts fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate at the committed glycolytic step. Glucose-6-phosphate can enter other pathways, while PFK-2 makes the regulatory metabolite fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.

questions.text: Glycolysis occurs in:
questions.explanation: Glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate using cytosolic enzymes. It can therefore generate ATP in mature erythrocytes, which have no mitochondria.

questions.text: True statement about glycolysis is:
questions.explanation: Glycolysis converts a six-carbon sugar into three-carbon units; it does not completely oxidize glucose to CO2.
options: 3 ATPs are used in anaerobic pathway

questions.text: The number of ATPs produced by glycolysis in RBC is........
questions.explanation: Glycolysis forms four ATP but uses two ATP in its investment phase, leaving two net ATP per glucose. Conversion of pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD+ without producing additional ATP.

questions.text: Whenever the cell's AMP supply is increased, which of the following enzyme's activity is increased?
questions.explanation: AMP signals low energy and allosterically activates PFK-1, increasing glycolytic flux.

questions.text: Two inhibitors of glycolysis.
questions.explanation: ATP inhibits PFK-1 when cellular energy is abundant; citrate also inhibits PFK-1 and signals sufficient mitochondrial carbon/energy supply.
questions.modelAnswer: ATP inhibits PFK-1 when cellular energy is abundant; citrate also inhibits PFK-1 and signals sufficient mitochondrial carbon/energy supply.
requiredPoints: ATP inhibits PFK-1 when cellular energy is abundant
citrate also inhibits PFK-1 and signals sufficient mitochondrial carbon/energy supply.

questions.text: Irreversible enzymes of glycolysis
questions.explanation: Hexokinase or glucokinase catalyzes glucose phosphorylation; PFK-1 phosphorylates fructose-6-phosphate; pyruvate kinase converts PEP to pyruvate. These are the three effectively irreversible glycolytic steps.
questions.modelAnswer: Hexokinase or glucokinase catalyzes glucose phosphorylation; PFK-1 phosphorylates fructose-6-phosphate; pyruvate kinase converts PEP to pyruvate. These are the three effectively irreversible glycolytic steps.
requiredPoints: Hexokinase or glucokinase catalyzes glucose phosphorylation
PFK-1 phosphorylates fructose-6-phosphate
pyruvate kinase converts PEP to pyruvate. These are the three effectively irreversible glycolytic steps.

questions.text: Glycolysis in liver cells can be inhibited by :
questions.explanation: High ATP inhibits phosphofructokinase-1 and slows glycolysis when energy is sufficient.

questions.text: What is the fate of NADH produced during glycolysis?
questions.explanation: The glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step requires NAD+, so glycolysis must regenerate it from NADH. Lactate formation or mitochondrial oxidation of transferred reducing equivalents supplies this regeneration.

questions.text: How many net ATP is produced in a case of genetic absence of pyruvate kinase in RBCs.
questions.explanation: Without pyruvate kinase, the two ATP generated by phosphoglycerate kinase offset the two initially invested; net glycolytic ATP is zero.

questions.text: Glycolysis under anaerobic condition ends by :-
questions.explanation: Anaerobic glycolysis yields two lactates and two net ATP per glucose while regenerating NAD+.

questions.text: The first oxidation-reduction reaction of glycolysis is
questions.explanation: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase oxidizes the aldehyde while reducing NAD+ to NADH, forming 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate. The other listed glycolytic reactions do not perform this NAD+-linked oxidation.

questions.text: Which of the following enzymes Cleave Fructose 1,6 bis phosphate into two molecules ?
questions.explanation: Aldolase splits six-carbon fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and dihydroxyacetone phosphate. Triose phosphate isomerase can then convert the latter to a second glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate.

questions.text: Fructose 1,6 bis phosphate activates
questions.explanation: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate provides feed-forward activation of pyruvate kinase, linking an early glycolytic intermediate to the final step. Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate instead activates PFK-1.

questions.text: Fructose 2,6 bis phosphate activates
questions.explanation: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate allosterically activates PFK-1, promoting glycolysis. It also opposes gluconeogenesis through inhibition of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.

questions.text: Fructose 2,6 bis phosphate is produced by
questions.explanation: PFK-2 phosphorylates fructose-6-phosphate to form the regulatory metabolite fructose-2,6-bisphosphate. PFK-1 instead makes fructose-1,6-bisphosphate as part of glycolysis.

questions.text: The most potent activator of PFK-1 is
questions.explanation: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate allosterically activates PFK-1, promoting glycolysis. It also opposes gluconeogenesis through inhibition of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.

questions.text: Conversion of glucose to glucose 6 phosphate in livers is by
questions.explanation: Both hexokinase and glucokinase can phosphorylate glucose in the liver. The higher Km of glucokinase favors glucose trapping when glucose is abundant, while hexokinase works at lower concentrations.

questions.text: One of the following is Substrate level phosphorylation reaction in glycolysis
questions.explanation: Substrate-level phosphorylation transfers phosphate directly from a high-energy glycolytic intermediate to ADP. Pyruvate kinase uses PEP and phosphoglycerate kinase uses 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate; succinate thiokinase belongs to the TCA cycle.

questions.text: One of the following is Substrate level phosphorylation reaction in glycolysis
questions.explanation: Substrate-level phosphorylation transfers phosphate directly from a high-energy glycolytic intermediate to ADP. Pyruvate kinase uses PEP and phosphoglycerate kinase uses 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate; succinate thiokinase belongs to the TCA cycle.

questions.text: Irreversible steps of Glycolysis are catalyzed by:
questions.explanation: Hexokinase or glucokinase, PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase catalyze the three effectively irreversible glycolytic steps. These are control points that gluconeogenesis bypasses using different enzymes; PGK and GAPDH are reversible.
options: Glucokinase, Pyruvate Kinase, Glyceraldehyde 3 Phosphate Dehydrogenase

questions.text: One of the following is cofactor for lactate dehydrogenase:
questions.explanation: Lactate dehydrogenase uses NADH to reduce pyruvate to lactate and regenerate NAD+. Its reversible lactate oxidation instead reduces NAD+ to NADH.

questions.text: ONE of the following catalyze irreversible reactions of glycolysis:
questions.explanation: Glucokinase uses ATP to trap glucose as glucose-6-phosphate in an effectively irreversible glycolytic step. Phosphoglycerate kinase and enolase catalyze reversible glycolytic reactions.

questions.text: All the following statements are true except
questions.explanation: Glucokinase has a relatively high capacity/Vmax and high Km, unlike low-Km hexokinase.
options: Glucokinase is induced by insulin during well-fed state
Glucokinase has low affinity to glucose
Hexokinase is inhibited by glucose 6- P

questions.text: All the following statements are true except
questions.explanation: Glucose-6-phosphate product inhibition restrains hexokinase but not glucokinase. This allows hepatic glucokinase to keep trapping abundant fed-state glucose for storage and metabolism.
options: Glucokinase is induced by insulin during well-fed state
Hexokinase has high affinity to glucose
Glucokinase is inhibited by glucose 6- P

questions.text: All the following statements are true except
questions.explanation: Glucagon-driven phosphorylation inhibits hepatic pyruvate kinase, conserving substrates for glucose production. Insulin favors the active dephosphorylated form, while fructose-1,6-bisphosphate provides feed-forward activation.
options: Pyruvate kinase is active in phosphorylated form
Pyruvate kinase is inhibited by high ATP
Pyruvate kinase is activated by fructose 1,6 Bis-P
Pyruvate kinase is induced by insulin

questions.text: The only pathway for energy production in RBCs is
questions.explanation: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and obtain ATP through glycolysis.

questions.text: How many ATP is produced in glycolysis by substrate level phosphorylation
questions.explanation: Glycolysis generates four ATP gross per glucose, two at phosphoglycerate kinase and two at pyruvate kinase; net yield is two after investment.

questions.text: The approximate total iron content of a typical adult human is:
questions.explanation: A typical adult contains about 3–4 g of iron, within the listed 3–5 g range. Most is in hemoglobin; total body iron varies with body size, sex and iron status.

sourceOccurrences.source: Formative quiz of Biochemistry for 1st week.pdf

questions.text: The iron-containing non-heme protein is:
questions.explanation: Ferritin stores iron in a mineral core without a heme group; catalase, cytochrome c and the usual heme peroxidases bind iron within heme.

sourceOccurrences.source: Formative quiz of Biochemistry for 1st week.pdf

questions.text: List three iron-containing non-heme proteins.
questions.explanation: Ferritin is a non-heme iron-storage protein; transferrin binds and transports iron in plasma; aconitase contains a non-heme iron-sulfur[4Fe-4S] cluster.

questions.text: Megaloblastic anemia is caused by the deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and causes megaloblastic anemia; iron deficiency instead usually causes microcytosis.

sourceOccurrences.source: Formative quiz of Biochemistry for 1st week.pdf

questions.text: Vitamin B12 absorption occurs in:
questions.explanation: The stomach supplies intrinsic factor, which binds B12 before the complex is absorbed by receptors in the terminal ileum. The stomach and duodenum help prepare B12 for absorption rather than being its principal absorption site.

sourceOccurrences.source: Formative quiz of Biochemistry for 1st week.pdf

questions.text: The active form of folic acid is ____ and is activated by the enzyme ____ in the human body.
questions.explanation: Reduced folates carry one-carbon units needed for nucleotide synthesis and amino acid metabolism.

questions.explanation: B12 supports homocysteine-to-methionine conversion and methylmalonyl-CoA-to-succinyl-CoA conversion.

questions.text: Pellagra is mostly due to deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Pellagra is caused by severe niacin deficiency, impairing NAD/NADP-dependent metabolism; vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy.

questions.text: Vitamin synthesized by the intestinal bacteria is:
questions.explanation: Intestinal bacteria synthesize vitamin K menaquinones. Vitamins A, C and D are not the offered gut bacterial synthesis product.

questions.text: Pernicious anemia is caused by deficiency of vitamin:
questions.explanation: Pernicious anemia impairs intrinsic-factor production and vitamin B12 absorption, producing B12 deficiency; it is not any generic dietary B12 deficiency.

questions.text: Which one of the following vitamins is not fat-soluble?
questions.explanation: Vitamin C is water-soluble. Vitamins A, D and K are fat-soluble.

questions.text: Which one of the following is not a manifestation of vitamin D deficiency?
questions.explanation: A normal head is not a characteristic abnormal manifestation of rickets. Vitamin-D-deficiency rickets can cause skull bossing/softening, chest deformity, spinal curvature and pelvic flattening; these findings are not present in every affected patient.
options: Vertebral column appears with kyphosis or scoliosis.

questions.text: Neural tube defect in fetus could be prevented by supplementation of the pregnant female with:
questions.explanation: Periconceptional folic acid reduces neural tube defect risk because folate supports nucleotide synthesis and rapidly dividing embryonic tissue.

questions.text: Which of the following vitamins acts as coenzyme for transamination reaction?
questions.explanation: PLP is the B6 coenzyme used by aminotransferases; niacin supplies NAD, biotin serves carboxylases, and TPP supports other carbon-transfer reactions.

questions.text: Disturbances in the coagulation process may be caused by deficiency or vitamin:
questions.explanation: Vitamin K supports γ-carboxylation needed for functional coagulation proteins; severe deficiency prolongs clotting and causes bleeding.

questions.text: In children, a severe deficiency of vitamin D causes:
questions.explanation: Vitamin D deficiency impairs bone mineralization. The pediatric disease is rickets, while adult defective mineralization is osteomalacia.

questions.text: Beriberi is caused by a deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Thiamine deficiency produces beriberi with neuropathy and, in the wet form, heart failure.

questions.text: Which of the following pairs is not correctly matched?
questions.explanation: Pellagra is associated with niacin deficiency rather than folate deficiency; the other three vitamin-disease pairings are standard.

questions.text: Which of these is a vitamin A precursor?
questions.explanation: Beta-carotene is a provitamin A carotenoid cleaved to vitamin A; cobalamin, pyridoxine and thiamine are B vitamins.

questions.text: Osteomalacia in adults is caused due to deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Insufficient vitamin D causes defective mineralization of adult osteoid, producing osteomalacia.

questions.text: The active form of vitamin D is
questions.explanation: Kidney hydroxylation forms active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol); calcidiol is the preceding 25-hydroxy metabolite.

questions.text: A fat-soluble vitamin that regulates blood clotting is
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is a fat-soluble cofactor needed for gamma-carboxylation of coagulation proteins. Deficiency reduces their functional activity and can cause bleeding.

questions.text: Deficiency of Vitamin C causes:
questions.explanation: Scurvy results from insufficient vitamin C and defective connective tissue; night blindness instead points to vitamin A deficiency.

questions.text: Vitamin C is required for the production and maintenance of:
questions.explanation: Vitamin C supports the collagen biosynthetic reactions required for connective-tissue integrity. Deficiency weakens vessels and impairs wound healing, explaining the characteristic scurvy manifestations.

questions.text: A deficiency of niacin causes:
questions.explanation: Severe niacin deficiency causes pellagra, classically involving skin, gastrointestinal tract and nervous system.

questions.text: Vitamin B-12 deficiency caused by lack of intrinsic factor is called:
questions.explanation: Autoimmune intrinsic-factor deficiency impairs B12 absorption and causes pernicious anemia.

questions.text: Vitamin C increases the intestinal absorption of:
questions.explanation: Ascorbate promotes absorption of nonheme iron from food. This differs from the other listed ions and helps explain why vitamin C deficiency can contribute to iron deficiency.

questions.text: The vitamin required as coenzyme for the action of transaminases is:
questions.explanation: Pyridoxal phosphate participates in aminotransferase amino-group transfer as the active B6 coenzyme.

questions.text: Pellagra preventing factor is:
questions.explanation: Niacin supplies NAD/NADP and prevents the deficiency syndrome pellagra.

questions.text: The vitamin required for the formation of hydroxyproline (in collagen) is
questions.explanation: Collagen hydroxylation produces hydroxyproline, and this vitamin C-dependent step supports stable connective tissue. Vitamin C deficiency therefore impairs collagen integrity and wound healing.

questions.text: Vitamin D:
questions.explanation: Vitamin D promotes intestinal calcium absorption; its active form is 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and it is fat-soluble.
options: It increases Ca2+ absorption from the intestine.

questions.text: Pantothenic acid (B5):
questions.explanation: Pantothenic acid is a constituent of coenzyme A, which carries acyl groups; B5 is water-soluble and does not supply the visual chromophore.
options: It has an essential role in vision

questions.text: Which one of these vitamins has antioxidant effect:
questions.explanation: Vitamin E is a lipid-soluble antioxidant that interrupts oxidative damage to lipids; the other three are chiefly metabolic coenzyme precursors.

questions.text: Sulfonamides are antagonists of:
questions.explanation: Sulfonamides inhibit bacterial folate synthesis by antagonizing the PABA pathway. They do not antagonize B6, K or B12.

questions.text: Vitamin C:
questions.explanation: Vitamin C deficiency damages collagen-dependent connective tissue, causing fragile vessels and bleeding gums. PLP is the active form of vitamin B6.
options: Its deficiency causes bleeding gums due to synthesis of abnormal collagen.

questions.text: Which vitamin deficiency may lead to megaloblastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency disrupts DNA synthesis and produces megaloblastic anemia; it can also cause neurologic injury.

questions.text: Which one of these vitamins is involved in calcium homeostasis?
questions.explanation: Vitamin D promotes calcium absorption and calcium/phosphate homeostasis. K helps activate bone proteins but is not the principal calcium-homeostasis hormone vitamin.

questions.text: Which statement about the elongation of the lagging strand during DNA replication is correct?
questions.explanation: Each lagging-strand Okazaki fragment grows 5′ to 3′ away from the fork and requires a short RNA primer. It is not synthesized continuously.
options: It is synthesized in a 3' --> 5' direction.
It progresses (grows) toward the replication fork.
It requires a short RNA primer to proceed.

questions.text: Which enzymes remove supercoiling in replicating DNA ahead of the replication fork?
questions.explanation: Topoisomerases transiently cut and reseal DNA to relieve supercoiling ahead of the fork; helicases separate the strands at the fork.

questions.text: During which phase of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?
questions.explanation: Nuclear DNA is duplicated during S phase, before G2 and mitosis.

questions.text: What is the role of topoisomerases in eukaryotic DNA replication?
questions.explanation: Topoisomerases relieve torsional strain through transient cleavage and resealing; DNA ligase seals persistent nicks between fragments.
options: Topoisomerase enzymes cut, uncoil and reseal the double stranded DNA
Topoisomerase enzymes bind to the origin of replication sites within double stranded DNA.
Topoisomerase enzymes open up the double stranded DNA at the replication fork.
Topoisomerase enzymes join the Okazaki fragments together with phosphodiester bonds.

questions.text: The direction of DNA synthesis is:
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase adds each incoming nucleotide to the growing strand’s 3′-OH, so synthesis proceeds 5′ to 3′.

questions.text: Okazaki fragments are formed during the synthesis of:
questions.explanation: Okazaki fragments are the short DNA products made discontinuously on the lagging strand, rather than mature RNA products.

questions.text: After formation of the replication fork:
questions.explanation: At a replication fork, the leading strand is synthesized continuously and the lagging strand as Okazaki fragments; both are synthesized 5′ to 3′.
options: One strand is synthesized continuously and the other discontinuously
RNA primer is required only for the synthesis of one new strand.

questions.text: One of the following is not involved in prokaryotic replication:
questions.explanation: Typical bacterial circular chromosomes lack telomeres and do not require telomerase; polymerases and primase are needed for bacterial replication.

questions.text: One of the following is not a characteristic of telomerase:
questions.explanation: Telomerase uses its intrinsic RNA template to extend the 3′ end of the telomeric template strand, enabling lagging-strand completion. It is not a leading-strand elongation polymerase.
options: Is present only in eukaryotic cells.

questions.text: In prokaryotes, DNA polymerase Ill is responsible for:
questions.explanation: Bacterial DNA polymerase III elongates both leading and lagging strands. The difference between those strands is continuous versus fragment-by-fragment synthesis, not use of separate principal polymerases.

questions.text: Prokaryotic RNA primer is formed by:
questions.explanation: Primase makes short RNA primers; DNA polymerase III extends them with DNA nucleotides.

questions.text: Eukaryotes differ from prokaryote in mechanism of DNA replication in:
questions.explanation: Eukaryotes primarily use polymerase ε for the leading strand and δ for lagging synthesis, whereas bacterial polymerase III copies both.
options: Use of DNA primer rather than RNA primer
Different enzyme for synthesis of lagging and leading strand

questions.text: The enzyme used to join nicks of DNA is:

questions.text: Okazaki fragments occur on the and are bonded together by

questions.text: Given that DNA polymerases are unable to synthesize DNA without a primer, what molecule serves as the primer for these enzymes during DNA replication?
questions.explanation: Primase supplies a short RNA primer with a free 3′-OH, allowing DNA polymerase to begin elongation.

questions.text: What is a promoter?
questions.explanation: A promoter is a DNA sequence recognized by the transcription machinery to initiate RNA synthesis; it is not an RNA site or a replication origin.
options: A specific sequence of DNA to which DNA polymerase binds.
A specific sequence of DNA to which RNA polymerase binds
A specific DNA sequence to which a restriction endonuclease binds.

questions.explanation: The RNA sequence is complementary to the template strand, while matching the coding strand apart from U replacing T.

questions.explanation: Rho participates in rho-dependent transcription termination. Sigma directs initiation, rather than termination.

questions.explanation: Sigma supplies promoter specificity and positions the bacterial polymerase to initiate transcription at an appropriate site.

questions.text: In eukaryotes, synthesis of mRNA is catalyzed by:
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase II transcribes nuclear protein-coding pre-mRNAs. Polymerase I makes most rRNAs and III makes tRNAs and 5S rRNA.

questions.explanation: The standard pre-mRNA maturation steps are 5′ capping, 3′ polyadenylation and intron splicing. Trimming is conventionally associated with tRNA/rRNA precursor processing or protein maturation; mRNA nevertheless undergoes cleavage during 3′-end formation.

questions.explanation: Splicing removes introns and joins exons; DNA ligase and RNA polymerase do not perform this RNA-processing reaction.

It is cutting of introns and joining of exons

questions.text: TBP stands for?

questions.text: What is the macromolecular complex that associates with introns during mRNA splicing?
